newsitem.title: CANADA: Prairie rail rates likely rise if deregulated-SWP.
newsitem.headline: Prairie rail rates likely rise if deregulated-SWP.

text.p: Prairie rail rates on grain and oilseed shipments to export position will likely rise if Canada ends its cap on rates when it reviews them in 1999, a Saskatchewan Wheat Pool official said.

"Lets assume the cap comes off in the 1999 review. A lot of people say the rate will come down. I don't think so, I think the rate structure will pop up," SWP manager of grain marketing Mark Zenuk told delegates at the Canada Grains Council meeting in Ottawa.
Rail rates from Moose Jaw, Sask, to the Pacific coast total C$35/tonne and C$49/tonne to Duluth, Minn., he said.
Rail rates across the U.S. border at Plentywood, Montana, to the Pacific coast total C$65/tonne and C$54/tonne to Duluth, Minn, Zenuk added.
"The U.S. system says it's worth C$65 to ship to the West coast and that's an open market system," Zenuk said.

"If the cap comes off (in 1999) single car freight rates will go up but the 25, 50 and 100 car rates won't go up as much so the elevators that can handle large car spots will fare better," Zenuk added.

There were 2,000 primary elevators across the Prairies in crop year 1985/86 (Aug/July) compared to 1,200 in 1996/97 with handling capacity declining to 6.5 million tonnes in the current year from 8.0 million tonnes in 1985/86, he said.
While rail rates were likely to rise in a free market Zenuk said incentive rates for large railcar spots ought to rise to match those offered across the border.
A 25-car train in the U.S. hauling grain to the West coast currently offers a C$5/tonne incentive rate compared to a 100-car train in Canada offering a C$3/tonne incentive rate, he said.
"The incentive rates have got to change," Zenuk said.
"Producers in western Canada are used to producing a lot of different crops and that adds to the problem because a lot of these special crops move in single car units," he said.
Pulse crops, for example, were expected to take up 2.0 million acres in Saskatchewan, more than oats or flax this spring, said Garth Patterson of the Saskatchewan Pulse Crop Development Board.
"I think you'll see fully integrated multinationals moving into the Prairies and privatization and consolidation will continue," SWP's Zenuk said.
"Land prices will be a function of proximity to transportation facilities and processing," he added.
